The two deliberately shared marking points, declared. First, heat stress makes coral polyps expel their zooxanthellae, so the coral loses its photosynthetic food supply and starves, which Q2(b) and Q2(c) need as mechanism and Q9 needs as one of thirteen possible marks in a category that requires two; the three are marked on different things, the sequence, the proximate trigger, and breadth across categories. Second, increased temperature raises insect metabolic rate and shortens the life cycle, which Q7(b) needs for caterpillars and Q8(b) needs as one of five impacts; Q7(b) is marked on tying it to a dated phenological shift and Q8(b) on breadth with a direction of change attached to each. Every other required answer in the set is unique.

Nothing from Book 9, and nothing from Cluster 1 or Cluster 3. The carbon cycle, carbon footprints and the greenhouse mechanism itself are Cluster 1 and are assumed here rather than retested. Food security, biodiversity of the tropics, the Aedes aegypti life cycle and the spread of dengue beyond the tropics are Cluster 3. Dengue virology, serotypes and the host immune response are Extension Topic A and are out of scope for Book 8 entirely.

Question 1 [6 marks]

(a) Which statement helps to explain the role of mangrove forests in mitigating the impact of climate change?

AMangrove roots form a dense mass that slows the flow of water, causing suspended organic material to settle out and become trapped in oxygen-poor sediments that limit further decomposition.
BThe roots of mangrove trees absorb organic carbon from sediments and store it in their cell walls in biomolecules such as lignin and cellulose that are highly resistant to chemical breakdown.
CWhen the leaves of mangroves die and fall, they are carried quickly to the sea where the carbon fixed in photosynthesis is trapped in deep ocean sediments before it can be released in the process of decomposition.
DMangrove forests provide a buffer zone between the sea and land which reduces the rate at which sea levels can rise as a result of the melting of the polar ice caps and retreat of glaciers to higher altitudes.

[1]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) Which statement helps to explain the role of mangrove forests in mitigating the impact of climate change? [1] [INFERRED: no official key]

1. A

(b) Explain your answer to (a), taking each of the four statements in turn. [4]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Explain your answer, taking each of the four statements in turn. [4] [INFERRED: no official key]

1. Why A is right. Mangroves mitigate climate change by acting as a long-term carbon sink. The tangled prop roots slow the water flow so suspended organic matter settles and is buried in waterlogged, anaerobic sediment, and the lack of oxygen prevents aerobic decomposers from respiring the organic matter, so the carbon is locked away for centuries instead of returning to the atmosphere as CO2. The oxygen-poor step is the mark-bearing one. Saying only that the roots trap sediment leaves out the mechanism.

2. Why B is wrong. Trees fix carbon from atmospheric CO2 by photosynthesis, not by absorbing organic carbon through their roots. The biomolecules named in the option are correct; the route into them is not.

3. Why C is wrong. The leaf litter is in fact retained within the mangrove sediment, not swept to the deep ocean.

4. Why D is wrong. D describes protection of the coast from the consequences of warming, which is adaptation rather than mitigation, and it is also factually wrong, because mangroves cannot slow the rate of sea level rise. They buffer waves and storm surge; the rate at which the sea rises is unaffected.

(c) In many tropical and subtropical regions, mangroves reduce waves and storm surges, and serve as a first line of defence against flooding and erosion. One study quantifies global mangrove benefits by estimating the difference in flood damages between two scenarios: one "with mangroves", the current global extent of mangroves, and another "without mangroves". Table 3.1 shows the land flooded, people and property damaged with and without mangroves across 700 000 km of mangrove coastlines globally. The difference between scenarios is the benefit provided by current mangroves.

Calculate the annual expected benefit of mangroves in terms of people affected and property loss and fill in your answers in Table 3.1. [1]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (c)

(c) Calculate the annual expected benefit of mangroves in terms of people affected and property loss. [1]

1. People affected = 15 million.

2. Property loss = 65 $US billion.

3. Both must be correct for 1 mark.

Part (b) is the drill's own follow-on, and that follow-on wording is itself lifted from real prelim papers that set "explain your answer" after an MCQ; the specimen ships without a mark scheme, so the reasoning is inferred and is built on the option text itself. ASRJC Prelim 2022 P3 Q3c(i), stem, table and key verbatim (c), with Fig. 3.2 dropped because the calculation does not need it. Archetype: the hardest MCQ shape in this Book, four full-paragraph mechanisms of which three are well-formed and plausible. It is only answerable by someone who knows why mangrove sediment stores carbon, not that it does. Trap: every distractor is a real misconception this Book records. B is uptake confused with fixation. C is the belief that mangrove litter is exported. D is buffering a consequence confused with mitigating a cause. A candidate who answers "roots trap sediment" and stops has given A's first clause and missed its second, which is the one that scores. Concepts fused: (1) mangroves as a long-term carbon sink; (2) root architecture slowing water and trapping sediment; (3) waterlogged anaerobic sediment limiting decomposition; (4) fixation of atmospheric CO2 against uptake of organic carbon; (5) retention against export of litter; (6) mitigation of the cause against adaptation to the consequence; (7) reading a benefit as a difference between two scenarios.

Question 2 [11 marks]

(a) Zooxanthellae are unicellular photosynthetic algae that reside in the cells of corals. The relationship between the zooxanthellae and the corals is known to be symbiotic. Describe how the relationship is symbiotic. [2]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) Describe how the relationship between zooxanthellae and corals is symbiotic. [2]

1. It is beneficial to the zooxanthellae as the corals provide nutrients and protection for the zooxanthellae.

2. It is beneficial to the coral as the zooxanthellae undergo photosynthesis to provide the corals with food.

3. Fuller versions of both directions: algae to coral, photosynthesis produces glucose, glycerol and amino acids, which provide most of the coral's food and nutrition; coral to algae, inorganic nitrogen and phosphorus from the polyp's metabolic waste, plus shelter and protection from excess ultraviolet radiation. Both directions must be stated for both marks.

(b) Rising sea surface temperatures have been suggested as a reason for more frequent coral bleaching events. Explain how an increase in sea surface temperature may lead to coral bleaching. [2]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Explain how an increase in sea surface temperature may lead to coral bleaching. [2]

1. Photosynthetic algae, the zooxanthellae, are sensitive to heat stress, especially when the temperature rises above a critical threshold.

2. The zooxanthellae will then be expelled by the corals, and coral bleaching occurs as the coral appears white, this being the natural white colour of the calcium carbonate which forms the coral skeleton.

3. Examiner's comment, verbatim: many students think zooxanthellae first die or have their enzymes denatured due to heat and are then expelled. That is mainly not true, as they are expelled while still alive. Death of corals does not lead to bleaching; rather, prolonged coral bleaching can lead to corals dying.

(c) Suggest why zooxanthellae are expelled by coral polyp epithelial cells when sea temperatures are high. [2]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (c)

(c) Suggest why zooxanthellae are expelled by coral polyp epithelial cells when sea temperatures are high. [2]

1. Zooxanthellae are no longer photosynthesising and producing food, therefore they are expelled.

2. H2O2 and reactive oxygen species produced by the zooxanthellae during photosynthesis diffuse into the cytoplasm of the coral inner epithelial cell and cause damage or death of the zooxanthellae or of the polyp epithelial cell.

(d) Corals are affected by climate change. Explain two factors, resulting from climate change, that could contribute to the death of corals. [5]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (d)

(d) Explain two factors, resulting from climate change, that could contribute to the death of corals. [5] [INFERRED: no official key]

1. Factor 1, rising sea surface temperature causing bleaching. Increased atmospheric concentrations of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases enhance the greenhouse effect and raise the mean sea surface temperature.

2. Above the coral's optimum temperature the symbiotic zooxanthellae living inside the coral's tissues become heat-stressed, their photosystems are damaged and they produce reactive oxygen species, so the coral expels them.

3. The coral loses its colour, which is the bleaching, and more importantly loses the products of photosynthesis supplied by the algae, which normally provide most of its organic carbon and energy. Without this supply the coral cannot respire, grow or repair itself, and if the high temperature persists the coral starves and dies.

4. Factor 2, ocean acidification, and this is the chain your notes get wrong. About a quarter of the additional atmospheric carbon dioxide dissolves in seawater and reacts with water to form carbonic acid, which dissociates and releases H⁺ ions, lowering the pH of the ocean. The extra H⁺ ions react with carbonate ions to form hydrogencarbonate ions, so the concentration of free carbonate ions in the water falls.

5. Corals need carbonate ions to deposit calcium carbonate for their exoskeleton, so the rate of calcification slows and existing skeletons begin to dissolve. The weakened skeleton is more easily broken by wave action and by boring organisms, so the coral colony breaks up and dies.

6. Alternative acceptable factors: rising sea level and increased storm intensity, which increase turbidity and sediment load so that less light reaches the zooxanthellae for photosynthesis, and changes in salinity caused by increased freshwater run-off from melting ice.

7. Two corrections to carry out of this part. Your notes say corals cannot absorb the calcium carbonate they need. Corals do not absorb calcium carbonate, they deposit it, taking up calcium ions and carbonate or hydrogencarbonate ions. And your notes say the ocean is about 30% more acidic than in 1751; pH is logarithmic, so it did not change by 30%. What rose about 30% is the hydrogen ion concentration, which is a pH fall of roughly 0.1 units.

Sources & concepts

Source: MI Prelim 2023 P3 Q3c, stem and key verbatim (a), with Fig. 3.1 dropped because the answer does not depend on it and the polyp description folded into the stem; NJC Prelim 2023 P3 Q3a, stem, key and the full examiner's comment verbatim (b), with Fig. 3.1's preamble reduced to the one sentence the part needs; ASRJC Prelim 2023 P3 Q3a(ii), stem and both marking points verbatim (c); SAJC Prelim 2025 P3 Q3c, stem verbatim (d), with Fig. 3.1 dropped because the part asks for mechanisms rather than data. SAJC ships no key for that part, so its marking points are inferred; the acidification chain in points 4 and 5 is the chain the prelim schemes give and is the version the topic examiner's guide records as demonstrably better than the school notes. Archetype: the full-cycle process question of this drill. Symbiosis both ways, then the bleaching sequence in order, then ocean acidification run end to end from dissolved CO2 to a dissolving skeleton. Mechanism explain-chain is 16% of this concept heading and the marks come one per link. Trap: killing the zooxanthellae before expelling them, which the examiner comment names as the commonest error; stating only one direction of the symbiosis; writing the acidification chain as "corals cannot absorb calcium carbonate", which is chemically wrong and is what your own notes print; and saying the pH fell by 30%. LOs: (b) stress to coral reef ecosystems, in all four parts; reach-back Core Idea 3 photosynthesis, and Core Idea 1 for the protein damage in (c). Concepts fused: (1) mutualism defined by benefit in both directions; (2) what passes each way in the coral symbiosis; (3) the bleaching threshold; (4) expulsion of living algae; (5) the white skeleton showing through; (6) reactive oxygen species as the proximate trigger; (7) starvation as the cause of death; (8) CO2 dissolving to carbonic acid; (9) dissociation releasing H⁺; (10) H⁺ removing carbonate ions; (11) calcification against dissolution of CaCO3; (12) turbidity and salinity as alternative stressors.

Question 3 [7 marks]

(a) The diagram shows some of the possible effects of global warming. Which effect of warming in the polar regions could help to reduce global warming, according to this diagram?

Aincreased moisture transport from tropical regions
Bincreased growth of vegetation
Cmelting of sea ice
Dearlier snow melt

[1]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) Which effect of warming in the polar regions could help to reduce global warming, according to this diagram? [1] [INFERRED: no official key]

1. A

(b) Explain your answer to (a), taking each of the four options in turn and saying what the diagram shows it leads to. [4]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Explain your answer, taking each of the four options in turn and saying what the diagram shows it leads to. [4] [INFERRED: no official key]

1. Why A is right. A is the only option that feeds "more clouds in summer", which is the one node on the diagram reached by an arrow labelled negative feedback. Clouds reflect incoming shortwave solar radiation back to space, so less is absorbed by the surface and the warming is reduced. The moisture that makes those clouds arrives both as increased evaporation over the warming polar ocean and as moisture transported from lower latitudes, and the diagram draws both routes into the same node.

2. Why B is wrong. The diagram runs increased growth of vegetation to decreased sun reflection, because dark vegetation replaces pale snow and tundra, then to increased absorption of heat by land, then to warming of land, which is on the arm the diagram labels positive feedback. It amplifies warming.

3. Why C is wrong. Melting of sea ice leads to decreased sun reflection, because dark open water replaces bright ice, then to increased absorption of heat by sea, then to warming of sea, again labelled positive feedback. This is the ice-albedo loop.

4. Why D is wrong. Earlier snow melt takes the same route as C but on land: decreased sun reflection, increased absorption of heat by land, warming of land, labelled positive feedback.

5. Note the wording tension and answer the diagram, not the phrasing. The stem says effect of warming in the polar regions, and moisture transport in the diagram originates from the temperate and tropical box, while the polar box's own route to the clouds is increased evaporation. B, C and D are unambiguously effects of polar warming and all three are unambiguously positive feedbacks, so A is the only option left that reduces warming. The examinable skill here is classifying a loop that is printed on the paper, not reciting the ice-albedo loop from memory.

(c) Melting permafrost in Siberia has revealed a well-preserved rhinoceros, with many of its internal organs still intact. Due to warming of the region, the permafrost is thawing, particularly during the summer months. Suggest how melting of the permafrost containing frozen organic matter could further contribute to climate change. [2]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (c)

(c) Suggest how melting of the permafrost containing frozen organic matter could further contribute to climate change. [2] [INFERRED: no official key]

1. Thawing exposes the trapped organic matter, which is the remains of dead plants and animals, to decomposers such as saprophytic bacteria and fungi that were previously inactive at sub-zero temperatures.

2. These decomposers respire the organic matter aerobically and release the carbon that had been locked away for thousands of years as carbon dioxide, and where the thawed ground is waterlogged and anaerobic, methanogenic archaea release methane instead.

3. Carbon dioxide and methane are greenhouse gases that absorb and re-radiate outgoing long-wave infra-red radiation back towards the Earth's surface, so the enhanced greenhouse effect raises the global mean temperature further.

4. This is a positive feedback loop, because the additional warming thaws still more permafrost, which releases still more greenhouse gas.

Sources & concepts

Source: 9477 Specimen Paper 1 Question 28, stem, diagram and all four options verbatim from the question paper, worth 1 mark on the real paper (a). The diagram is the specimen's own. Part (b) is the drill's own follow-on. The specimen ships without a mark scheme, so the letter and all reasoning are inferred; the classifications in (b) are read directly off the labels printed on the diagram. SAJC Prelim 2025 P3 Q2a, stem verbatim (c), key inferred because SAJC ships no key for that part. Archetype: network reading. The candidate is handed a feedback web with two positive feedbacks and one negative feedback already labelled and must classify an effect against it. This is why memorising the ice-albedo loop is not sufficient preparation for this outcome. Trap: picking C because the ice-albedo loop is the one you revised, when the diagram itself labels that arm positive; forgetting that vegetation growth darkens a bright surface and therefore warms it; and answering (c) with "permafrost releases greenhouse gases" without the decomposer step or the aerobic against anaerobic split that decides which gas. LOs: (b) melting of polar ice caps, and release of greenhouse gases from frozen organic matter; reach-back Core Idea 3 decomposition, aerobic and anaerobic respiration. Concepts fused: (1) positive against negative feedback; (2) albedo and surface reflectivity; (3) darkening by vegetation as well as by open water; (4) cloud as a reflector of incoming shortwave radiation; (5) permafrost as a frozen organic carbon store; (6) microbial decomposition reactivated by thaw; (7) aerobic decomposition giving CO2 and anaerobic giving CH4; (8) absorb and re-emit as the greenhouse mechanism; (9) self-amplifying loops.

Question 4 [10 marks]

(a) Researchers have been monitoring and recording the global sea level every year. Fig. 11.2 shows the change in sea level compared to the average sea level from 1993 to 2008, across the years from 1960 to 2022. Explain the changes in global sea level as seen in Fig. 11.2. [3]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) Explain the changes in global sea level as seen in Fig. 11.2. [3]

1. Quote the data, worth 1 mark. From 1960 to 2020 or 2022, the change in sea level compared to the 1993 to 2008 average increased from -60 mm to 80 mm. Accept a range of -70 to -60 mm and of 80 to 90 mm.

2. Increase in greenhouse gas emissions.

3. Causes the atmosphere to absorb and trap more infrared radiation or heat.

4. Which causes melting of polar ice caps and glaciers.

5. Thermal expansion of water.

6. Marking is the data point plus any two of points 2 to 5, each worth half a mark in the original scheme. Note that thermal expansion is the larger of the two physical causes, and that only land ice raises sea level, because floating sea ice already displaces its own mass of water.

(b) Global warming has changed both the thickness and surface area of sea ice of the Arctic Ocean as well as the Southern Ocean that surrounds Antarctica. Sea ice is highly sensitive to changes in temperature. Scientists calculated a long-term mean for the surface area of sea ice in each ocean and used it as a reference to examine changes in ice extent. Fig. 11.1 shows the variations from this mean, drawn as a zero line, over a period of time. The Antarctic trend line lies above the zero line and slopes gently upward with large year-to-year fluctuations about it, while the Arctic trend line falls steeply below the zero line over the same period with smaller fluctuations.

Distinguish between changes in the surface area of sea ice in the Arctic and Antarctica. [2]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Distinguish between changes in the surface area of sea ice in the Arctic and Antarctica. [2]

1. Any two of the following.

2. In the Arctic Ocean, the surface area of sea ice has declined; in the Antarctic, the surface area of sea ice has increased.

3. The rate of change in the surface area of sea ice is greater for the Arctic Ocean than for the Southern Ocean around the Antarctic.

4. There are greater fluctuations in the surface area of sea ice in the Southern Ocean around the Antarctica than in the Arctic Ocean.

(c) Climate change results in global warming which affects both land and water masses. Scientists measured the change in mean land surface air temperature and mean sea surface air temperature from 1980 to 2018. Both rise, but the land surface curve rises more steeply and lies above the sea surface curve, the gap between them reaching 0.6 °C by 2018.

Other than heat capacity, explain the difference between the change in the two mean surface air temperatures from 1980. [2]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (c)

(c) Other than heat capacity, explain the difference between the change in the two mean surface air temperatures from 1980. [2]

1. Mean land surface air temperature increases more rapidly than mean sea surface air temperature, from 1980 to 2018, by 0.6 °C.

2. There is more heat retained or less heat radiated to the atmosphere by land, due to greater deforestation resulting in lack of cover or reduced transpiration, or due to urbanisation resulting in more urban heat islands.

(d) Suggest how the melting of snow and glaciers on the Himalayan mountains could increase stress on freshwater supplies. [1]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (d)

(d) Suggest how the melting of snow and glaciers on the Himalayan mountains could increase stress on freshwater supplies. [1]

1. Less ice melt or water is contributed to the rivers after the initial melt, leading to rivers drying up.

2. Increased pumping of underground water or aquifers worsens freshwater stress.

3. An additional valid point is that pollutants, for example DDT, trapped in ice that melts rapidly could contaminate freshwater.

(e) India has been facing freshwater shortage issues for decades, and climate change has made water scarcity a persistent and pressing issue. Fig. 11.1 plots water demand and water supply in billion cubic metres against year. Demand rises from about 500 in 1990 to about 1150 in 2020 and a projected 1500 in 2030, while supply falls from about 1250 in 1990 to about 1050 in 2020 and a projected 840 in 2030.

Explain how climate change can result in the projected water supply in Year 2030. [2]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (e)

(e) Explain how climate change can result in the projected water supply in Year 2030. [2]

1. An increase in global temperature or global warming results in excessive evaporation, drying up reservoirs or water storage facilities.

2. The shrinking of glaciers results in reduction of meltwater supplies.

3. It can alter precipitation patterns and hydrological systems in many regions, which can result in droughts and thus reduce water supply.

Sources & concepts

Source: TJC Prelim 2025 P2 Q11b, stem and full key verbatim including the tolerance ranges (a); Fig. 11.2 could not be recovered because the TJC 2025 papers are not in the inputs archive, so the figure carries the source paper's own description. CJC Prelim 2023 P2 Q11a, stem and all three alternative marking points verbatim (b), with the Fig. 11.1 description folded into the stem for the same reason. RVHS Prelim 2023 P2 Q11a, stem and key verbatim (c), with the Fig. 11.1 description folded into the stem. ASRJC Prelim 2023 P2 Q11d, stem and key verbatim (d). VJC Prelim 2023 P2 Q11b, stem and key verbatim (e), with the Fig. 11.1 figures folded into the stem so the part stands without Q11(a). Archetype: LO (b)'s named effects run as short causal chains, each attached to a real data set. Four of the outcome's eight named effects appear here: melting of polar ice caps, rising sea levels, stress on fresh water supplies, and the underlying temperature asymmetry that drives them. Trap: giving meltwater as the only cause of sea level rise and omitting thermal expansion, which the school's own notes call the main cause; letting melting sea ice raise sea level, when floating ice already displaces its own mass; explaining the land-against-ocean warming gap with heat capacity, which the stem rules out by name; and describing the 2030 supply projection without naming a mechanism. LOs: (b) melting of polar ice caps, rising sea levels, stress on fresh water supplies, extreme weather. Concepts fused: (1) sea level anomaly against a baseline period; (2) thermal expansion of warming seawater; (3) land ice against sea ice; (4) hemispheric asymmetry in sea ice trends; (5) variability against trend; (6) land warming faster than ocean; (7) deforestation and urban heat islands as land-specific drivers; (8) the temporary glacier-melt surplus followed by permanent deficit; (9) evaporation, altered precipitation and drought as supply-side losses.

Question 5 [10 marks]

(a) Fig. 11.1 shows the percentage cover of live corals, coral transplant by man and the temperature of the sea surface over 40 years. Using Fig. 11.1, describe the change in sea surface temperature and the percentage coverage of live corals. [3]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) Using Fig. 11.1, describe the change in sea surface temperature and the percentage coverage of live corals. [3]

1. From 1980 to 1990 there is a slight decrease of coral coverage from 100% to 90% as sea surface temperature rises from 26.1 to 26.5 °C.

2. A steep decline of 90% to 36% in the coral coverage from 1990 to 2005 as the temperature rises from 26.8 to 28 °C.

3. A gradual decrease in coral of 36% to 24% as temperature continues to increase from 28 to 28.9 °C between 2005 and 2020.

4. The scheme's granularity rule, verbatim: Each point must include duration, coral coverage % and temperature in °C. No mark is awarded for any point where the wrong graph or axis is read from.

5. Examiner's comment, verbatim: students must make fair comparative data analysis containing duration in years, temperature and coral coverage in each set; a common mistake was reading off the wrong axes and graphs.

(b) Using the information provided, explain whether coral transplanting is a successful strategy to combat shrinking coral habitat. [3]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Using the information provided, explain whether coral transplanting is a successful strategy to combat shrinking coral habitat. [3]

1. Take the stance: not successful. Corals are temperature sensitive, and from the data it suggests that they do not thrive when the sea surface temperature exceeds 26 °C.

2. Corals are bleached when the temperature exceeds 26 °C.

3. The temperature of the sea is continuously increasing, so transplanted coral is being placed into water that keeps getting warmer, and coral transplanting rises to about 35% over the same period in which live coral cover still falls to about 24%.

(c) Reef-building corals harbour algal symbionts from the genus Symbiodinium, and colonies of Pocillopora damicornis are dominated by Symbiodinium from genetically distinct groups, C or D. Fig. 9.1 shows the symbiont cell densities, as algal cell mass per gram of coral tissue, in colonies dominated by group C (open circles, dashed line) and group D (filled circles, solid line) at each time point during the warming period and the bleaching event. The mean water temperature experienced by the corals over the 14-day period preceding each sampling point is shown as the middle line of the box plots.

Describe and explain the relationship between mean water temperature and the trend observed for symbiont cell densities during the warming period. [3]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (c)

(c) Describe and explain the relationship between mean water temperature and the trend observed for symbiont cell densities during the warming period. [3]

1. The increase in mean temperature from 23.5 °C to 28.0 °C during the warming period saw a corresponding increase in symbiont cell density from 0.06 a.u. to 0.15 a.u. for colonies with clade D, and from 0.04 a.u. to 0.07 a.u. for colonies with clade C, with values quoted correctly.

2. The increase in temperature leads to higher metabolism for the algal cells due to greater enzyme activity, or a greater rate of photosynthesis or respiration, hence greater growth rates and higher cell density.

(d) Suggest why, although there was no change in temperature between 13 and 18 August, there was a decrease in symbiont cell density. [1]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (d)

(d) Suggest why, although there was no change in temperature between 13 and 18 August, there was a decrease in symbiont cell density. [1]

1. Prolonged exposure to elevated temperatures caused corals to undergo a prolonged period of stress resulting in bleaching.

2. 31 °C is already beyond the thermal tolerance.

3. There were additional stress factors due to climate change like increased bacterial infection, lower pH due to ocean acidification.

Sources & concepts

Source: YIJC Prelim 2025 P2 Q11a, stem, figure, all three marking points, the granularity rule and the examiner's comment verbatim (a); YIJC Prelim 2025 P2 Q11b, stem and all three marking points verbatim (b). RI Prelim 2023 P2 Q9a, stem, figure and key verbatim (c), with the study preamble kept and the bleaching-event definition moved into (d) where it is needed; RI Prelim 2023 P2 Q9d, stem and all three alternative marking points verbatim (d). Archetype: the data-granularity block of this Book. "With reference to" or "use the data" opens, nearly double Book 3, and a quarter of the structured marks are gated on quoting data correctly. Question 5(a) is the single clearest statement anywhere in the papers of what a quote has to contain. Trap: describing the trend without values, units or intervals; reading a value off the wrong y-axis when two are printed; treating the rise in symbiont density during the warming period as if it were already bleaching, when it is the opposite, growth accelerating with temperature; and assuming that a flat temperature means a flat stress, when it is the duration of the exposure that does the damage. LOs: (b) stress to coral reef ecosystems; reach-back Core Idea 1 LO (q) enzymes and temperature for the growth response in (c). Concepts fused: (1) reading two y-axes against one x-axis; (2) quoting duration, value and unit for every point; (3) segmenting a trend into intervals with different gradients; (4) judging an intervention against the trend it is meant to reverse; (5) genetically distinct symbiont groups with different thermal tolerance; (6) temperature raising algal metabolic and growth rate below the threshold; (7) cumulative exposure time as a stressor independent of temperature; (8) additional stressors acting together.

Question 6 [11 marks]

(a) Mount Gongga, the highest mountain in the Hengduan Mountains, is located in Sichuan province, China. It has an elevation of 7556 m above sea level. On Mount Gongga, regions with higher elevation experience lower temperatures and increased precipitation. Scientists conducted a long-term study to investigate the effect of changes to climate on elevation shifts of the plants on Mount Gongga. To determine the mean elevation of each plant species in 1950 they obtained historical data from the National Specimen Information Infrastructure and the Chinese Virtual Herbarium, and in 2018 they conducted a comprehensive field survey to determine the mean elevation of the same species. There were 83 species of plants in total with data for both 1950 and 2018, and all other plant species with incomplete data were excluded. It is estimated that the rapid climate warming in this area started during 1985 to 1990.

Using the data in Fig. 10.1, explain how climate change affects plant distribution. [3]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) Using the data in Fig. 10.1, explain how climate change affects plant distribution. [3]

1. Upward shift. The majority, 53 species of plant, experience an upward shift in mean elevation, where mean elevation in 2018 is greater than mean elevation in 1950.

2. Because climate change leads to increased temperature or decreased precipitation exceeding tolerable limits.

3. The range shifts upwards, towards higher altitude, where there is decreased temperature and increased precipitation which is now within tolerable limits.

4. No change. 11 plant species experienced no change to mean elevation, because the changes to temperature or precipitation that occur are still within tolerable limits.

5. Downward shift. A few, 19, plant species experienced a downhill shift in mean elevation, because of changes in species compositions and increased competition in the communities located at high altitudes, forcing smaller populations of species to move downhill.

6. Maximum 2 marks from the three data-quoting points 1, 4 and 5. The explanation points are where the rest of the marks are.

(b) Suggest why it would be difficult for the scientists to conclude that the changes in mean elevation for the plant species were due to climate change. [2]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Suggest why it would be difficult for the scientists to conclude that the changes in mean elevation for the plant species were due to climate change. [2]

1. Any two.

2. Difficulties in determining cause and effect. There could have been other factors affecting the range shifts other than climate, and there are difficulties in determining whether the increase in temperature or warming was due to climate change or other factors. Accept correlation does not mean causation.

3. Historical data had to be used, which may not be as accurate or reliable.

4. There may have been incomplete data.

5. Reject "sample size is too small".

(c) The foxglove Digitalis purpurea is a common plant in many parts of the world. Foxglove plants are naturally found at the bases of mountains, at sea level, up to the sub-alpine regions at about 2000 m in Europe. Based on the information above, explain how climate change might alter the distribution of foxglove plants. [3]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (c)

(c) Explain how climate change might alter the distribution of foxglove plants. [3]

1. Expected change. There will be a range shift to cooler altitudes up the mountains, and the plants may become locally extinct in warmer regions at sea level. Alternatively, the species will experience range contraction as it continually loses area at the low elevation part of its range but does not gain elevation at the high end.

2. Explanation. An increase in temperatures at lower altitudes may cause, for example, enzyme denaturation, affecting metabolism. Accept the converse, that at higher altitudes the temperature is within the optimum of the enzyme.

3. It may affect reproductive success, flowering or germination.

4. Any valid point is credited, for example water stress, since increased temperatures tend to occur with low precipitation, causing stomatal closure to prevent excessive loss of water through transpiration, a lower photosynthesis rate, and slower plant growth or plant death.

(d) Climate change also results in more extreme weather conditions. Describe the effects of such environmental stress on food chains and niche occupation. [3]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (d)

(d) Describe the effects of extreme weather as environmental stress on food chains and niche occupation. [3]

1. On food chains. Floods or droughts can harm producers and reduce yield.

2. There is reduced prey availability for predators.

3. Removal of predators can result in prey population explosion.

4. Heat waves can decrease population through increased disease vulnerability, reduced fertility or reduced milk production.

5. On niche occupation. There is increased competition intensity due to reduced resource availability.

6. It may result in niche alteration due to changes in behaviour.

7. There may be niche expansion or contraction.

8. Any other valid point is accepted. Keep the vocabulary apart: a habitat is the physical place an organism lives, while an ecological niche is its total way of life, including every environmental factor it needs to grow, survive and reproduce.

Sources & concepts

Source: School (HCI) Prelim 2023 P2 Q10a, stem and full key verbatim including the max-2 restriction (a); Fig. 10.1 could not be recovered, because the scatter plot on that page of the HCI paper does not render or extract as an image, so the figure carries the paper's own description. School (HCI) Prelim 2023 P2 Q10b, stem, key and the reject line verbatim (b). ASRJC Prelim 2025 P2 Q6d, stem and full key verbatim (c), with the foxglove genetics context from the parent question dropped because this part does not use it. RVHS Prelim 2023 P2 Q11b, stem and full key verbatim (d). Archetype: the most figure-led block in the whole Biology the papers. The habitats and niches heading runs at 61% data and figure interpretation. Reciting a case study is not what gets tested here; reading a new range shift off a new figure is. Trap: explaining only the majority upward shift and ignoring the 11 species that did not move and the 19 that moved down, which is where the explanation marks are; quoting three data points and expecting three marks, when the scheme caps data at 2; giving a change of distribution in (c) with no physiological mechanism behind it; and answering (d) with habitat loss when the stem asks specifically for food chains and niche occupation. LOs: (f) effects of increased environmental stress on habitats, organisms, food chains and niche occupation, in all four parts; reach-back Core Idea 1 LO (q) enzymes and temperature, and LO (l) water movement, in (c). Concepts fused: (1) a line of equality as the test for a shift; (2) tolerance limits set by temperature and precipitation; (3) upslope tracking of a moving isotherm; (4) species that do not move because the change stays inside their limits; (5) competition forcing a downhill shift against the temperature expectation; (6) correlation against causation, and the limits of historical data; (7) range contraction when there is no ground left above; (8) enzyme denaturation as the physiological limit; (9) stomatal closure and reduced carbon fixation under water stress; (10) food chain effects through producers and through predator removal; (11) niche expansion, contraction and alteration.

Question 7 [10 marks]

North America is home to diverse migratory bird species that travel long distances between their breeding grounds in the north and wintering grounds in the south. One such migratory bird species is the American robin. During the winter season, the robins migrate from the northern region of Canada to the southern region to seek their food source, caterpillars. Over the years, climate change has impacted the population of American robins, their migration pattern, and possibly their survival.

(a) Climate change has been said to affect the migratory phenology of the American robins. With reference to Fig. 3.1 and Fig. 3.2, describe and explain how climate change has caused the change in the migration pattern. [3]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) With reference to Fig. 3.1 and Fig. 3.2, describe and explain how climate change has caused the change in the migration pattern. [3]

1. From 1950 to 2000 there was an increase in the average global temperature, from 13.8 °C to 14.8 °C, due to global warming.

2. The migration of the robins was delayed by about 1 month, from September to October in 1950, to October to November in 2000.

3. Global warming resulted in warmer winters or a delayed onset of winter, during which food resources remain available, and this might have postponed the robins' migration or departure from southern Canada.

(b) Explain why the caterpillars are found in abundance earlier as shown in Fig. 3.3. [2]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Explain why the caterpillars are found in abundance earlier as shown in Fig. 3.3. [2]

1. The increase in global temperature can increase enzymatic activity or the metabolic rate of the insect, which speeds up developmental time.

2. This can result in the shortening of the life cycle of the insect, resulting in caterpillars emerging from the egg much sooner, from September to October in 1950 to August to September in 2000.

3. A bonus route in one of the two schemes, not required: the rise in global temperatures may also cause plants to produce new leaves sooner, which provides food for caterpillars earlier in the season, leading to their earlier abundance.

(c) Discuss how the changes shown in Fig. 3.2 and Fig. 3.3 can impact the American robins. [3]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (c)

(c) Discuss how the changes shown in Fig. 3.2 and Fig. 3.3 can impact the American robins. [3]

1. Global warming causes caterpillars to become abundant earlier, while robins migrate later, leading to a mismatch in timing.

2. By the time the robins arrive in southern Canada, their main food source is already depleted, as the caterpillars might have pupated or metamorphosed into adult butterflies, reducing the robins' chances of survival and successful breeding.

3. As a result, the robins may be forced to fly further south or rely on alternative food sources to survive.

4. The parallel scheme for the same question splits the reasoning into five separately creditable points: the robins migrate later while the caterpillars are in abundance earlier; this results in the lack of a food source for robins as they arrive at south Canada; the lack of food source can result in reduced viability of the robins at south Canada; robins might need to fly further south to find a region with a food source; robins might need to find other food sources in the region in order to survive.

5. The general rule this case rehearses: a phenological mismatch arises because two interacting species use different environmental cues, one tracking temperature and one not. That transfers to any predator-prey or plant-pollinator pair an examiner invents.

(d) In the mountains of North America, when winter changes into spring, the coat colour of snowshoe hares changes from white to brown. The change in coat colour occurs when new fur replaces old fur, and this is called moulting. Climatic changes have caused the snow to melt earlier, and this has reduced the survival rate of snowshoe hares in these habitats. Suggest and explain how. [2]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (d)

(d) Suggest and explain how climatic change has reduced the survival rate of snowshoe hares in mountain habitats. [2]

1. Snow melts earlier, or there is less snow, so there is less camouflage.

2. The hares which have yet to moult, the white hares, are more easily seen, eaten or killed by predators, or by any named example of a predator.

Sources & concepts

Source: CJC Prelim 2025 P3 Q3a, stem, Fig. 3.1, Fig. 3.2 and key verbatim, with the parallel VJC Prelim 2023 P3 Q3b wording of the last point noted (a); CJC Prelim 2025 P3 Q3b, stem, Fig. 3.3 and key verbatim, with the VJC Prelim 2023 P3 Q3c two-point version noted (b); CJC Prelim 2025 P3 Q3c, stem and key verbatim at 3 marks, with the VJC Prelim 2023 P3 Q3d five-point 4-mark key given in full (c); SAJC Prelim 2023 P2 Q10b, stem and key verbatim (d), with the moulting explanation kept and the population-level research finding dropped because this part does not use it. This is the shape the papers like most on LO (f) and it is the one where reciting the caribou case from the notes earns nothing. Trap: explaining the robin shift and the caterpillar shift separately and never putting them together, which is the whole of (c); assuming both species respond to the same cue, when the point is that they do not; and giving "less camouflage" in (d) without the predation consequence. Concepts fused: (1) phenology as the timing of seasonal activity; (2) different cues for interacting species; (3) temperature raising insect development rate and shortening the life cycle; (4) warmer or delayed winter retaining food and delaying migration; (5) mismatch as an emergent property of two shifts in opposite directions; (6) the prey life stage passing before the predator arrives; (7) behavioural compensation, flying further or switching food; (8) camouflage mismatch as a selection pressure.

Question 8 [12 marks]

(a) Climate change influences how mosquito-borne diseases such as dengue, chikungunya and zika infection have spread across the world through vectors such as mosquitoes. These mosquitoes generally have a narrow temperature tolerance. The effects of temperature on the rate of reaction are expressed as the temperature coefficient (Q10). Changes in temperature affect enzyme activity, which will affect an insect's growth and development.

Define what is Q10 theory and explain why insects have a narrow temperature tolerance range as compared to mammals. [2]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) Define what is Q10 theory and explain why insects have a narrow temperature tolerance range as compared to mammals. [2]

1. The Q10 theory of enzyme action states that for every rise of 10 °C there is a two-fold increase in enzyme action.

2. Mosquitoes are ectothermic, having a body temperature the same as the ambient temperature, and any extreme temperature beyond the physiological tolerance of that insect may be lethal.

3. The contrast the part wants: endotherms actively control core body temperature and can raise internal heat production in response to cold, whereas ectotherms have no direct way to regulate core temperature and depend on their environment, using behaviour such as basking or shading.

(b) Outline how an increase in temperature as a result of global warming can impact insects. [5]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Outline how an increase in temperature as a result of global warming can impact insects. [5]

1. Any five of the following.

2. Insects have a narrow temperature tolerance range, hence might die.

3. There may be migration of insects to higher altitudes.

4. There may be a shift of insect activity range northwards and southwards.

5. Insects may have higher metabolic rates and hence higher activity rates.

6. Hence they may have shorter life cycles.

7. They may be smaller in size if they grow faster.

8. There may be a higher rate of mating, and hence this may increase reproduction rates, increasing their numbers and dispersion range.

9. Any other valid point.

10. The examiner comment that decides this question, verbatim from a parallel scheme on the same outcome: this question was poorly done where the majority did not provide explanations but merely stated the impacts. Students should note that using the term "affect" is vague, and they should specify the direction of change, for example increase or decrease, instead. That scheme pairs every effect with its consequence: increased metabolic rate gives increased activity, increased reproductive rate, shortened maturation and increased population size.

11. And the half of LO (h) that a monotonic answer misses: the outcome names increased temperature leading to increased metabolism and the narrow temperature tolerance of insects. The curve peaks and falls away on both sides. Warmer does not simply mean more insects.

Males of this species have a lower tolerance to higher temperatures than females. Explain how global warming might affect the population and distribution of these ladybirds. [3]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (c)

(c) Explain how global warming might affect the population and distribution of these ladybirds. [3]

1. Melanic morphs will be selected against as the global temperature increases, because they gain heat more easily.

2. There will be more females than males, as males have a lower tolerance to higher temperatures.

3. Melanic morphs will migrate northward further up Europe, due to the lower temperature there.

(d) Snakes are ectothermic reptiles. Suggest reasons for the change in number of snakes from 1980 to 2020. [2]

(d) Suggest reasons for the change in number of snakes from 1980 to 2020. [2]

Question 9 [13 marks]

Discuss the effects of climate change (as a result of greenhouse gas emissions). [13]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer

Discuss the effects of climate change (as a result of greenhouse gas emissions). [13]

1. Emission of greenhouse gases results in global warming, which causes the melting of ice sheets and sea ice.

2. Rise in sea level, any two. Melting of ice sheets results in extra water entering the ocean, leading to an increase in sea level. Melting of sea ice can lead to a positive feedback loop which further accelerates the melting of polar ice caps. As oceans become warmer, the water also expands, increasing the volume of the ocean water and leading to a further rise in sea level. Low-lying islands and coastal regions may become submerged.

3. Stress on fresh water supplies, any one pair. Many island nations will have their supplies of drinking water reduced because sea water will invade their freshwater aquifers. Melting of fresh water, that is ice sheets, into the sea also turns the already scarce fresh water into salt water, decreasing the freshwater availability. Global warming also results in more evaporation, which leads to an increased amount of water in the atmosphere and hence heavier rainfall, which leads to more rapid movement of water from the atmosphere back to the oceans, reducing our ability to store and use it. At higher temperature, more precipitation will occur as rain rather than snow. Reservoirs fill quickly to maximum capacity, and any excess rain water is lost as runoff which cannot be stored, so less water will penetrate the ground surface, causing reduced soil moisture and reduced groundwater replenishment.

4. Heat waves and heavy rains, any two. A warmer climate creates an atmosphere that can collect, retain and drop more water, changing weather patterns. This causes wet areas to become wetter and dry areas to become drier, and can lead to heat waves and heavy rain. Heatwaves associated with low humidity may result in wildfire. Heavy rain increases the amount of runoff into rivers and lakes, washing sediment, nutrients, pollutants, trash, animal waste and other materials into water supplies, making them unusable, unsafe, or in need of water treatment.

5. Death of coral reefs, any two. Heat stress can cause coral bleaching, in which coral polyps expel the zooxanthellae. This is because at higher temperatures zooxanthellae photosynthesis is disrupted and the zooxanthellae produce more toxic compounds. If temperatures remain above the bleaching threshold for prolonged periods of time, corals will eventually die from starvation and disease. Ocean acidification affects hard corals as they cannot absorb the calcium carbonate to maintain their skeletons, and the stony skeletons that support corals will dissolve.

6. Migration of fishes and insects, any two. Rising ocean temperatures can directly affect the metabolism, life cycle and behaviour of marine species. Many fish species, especially their young and larvae, have highly specific temperature ranges and will move to cooler waters to survive. Warmer temperatures may disrupt the migratory behaviour and timing of several fish species, for example by impeding their ability to orient themselves for effective navigation. Insect distribution and migration are also greatly influenced by increased temperatures, as they are cold-blooded and will move to habitats with temperatures that are optimal for their growth and reproduction. These insect migrations have ramifications for many ecosystems, because insects play important ecological functions such as pollination, acting as vectors of diseases and parasites, killing other pest insects, or being crop pests themselves.

7. Release of greenhouse gases in frozen organic matter. Global warming leads to accelerated melting of permafrost. As permafrost thaws, the frozen organic matter starts to decay and is digested by microbes, and the digestion releases carbon dioxide and methane.

8. QWC: obtain at least 1 mark each from 3 different categories of effects of climate change.

9. Note the one line in this scheme that its own Book contradicts. Point 5's last clause says corals cannot absorb the calcium carbonate they need. That is the school's phrasing and it is chemically wrong: corals deposit calcium carbonate from calcium ions and carbonate ions, and what acidification removes is the free carbonate. Write the chain from Question 2(d), not this clause.

Sources & concepts

Source: SAJC Prelim 2017 P3 Section B Q4b, stem and the entire mark scheme verbatim including every category heading, every "any two" restriction and the QWC line, at its real 13 marks. This is one of three open "discuss the effects of climate change" sweeps of LO (b) among the 17 essay-scale Book 8 stems in the papers. Archetype: the LO (b) sweep. The outcome names eight effects and the examiner samples from the list, so the examinable unit is the chain, not the label. Note how the scheme is organised: five categories, each requiring one or two chains, and a QWC condition that forces breadth across at least three categories. Trap: listing the eight effects as labels with no causal links, which scores nothing; going deep on coral and never reaching three categories, which fails QWC; letting melting sea ice raise sea level; and reproducing the scheme's own faulty calcium carbonate clause. LOs: (b) in full, all eight named effects; reach-back Core Idea 3 decomposition in the permafrost category and Core Idea 1 enzymes in the migration category. Concepts fused: (1) greenhouse emission to warming as the common first link; (2) ice sheet melt against thermal expansion; (3) the ice-albedo positive feedback; (4) saltwater intrusion into aquifers; (5) a warmer atmosphere holding more water vapour; (6) wet areas wetter and dry areas drier; (7) runoff outpacing storage and carrying pollutants; (8) bleaching by expulsion of zooxanthellae; (9) acidification against the skeleton; (10) narrow thermal tolerance driving fish and insect range shifts; (11) insects as pollinators, vectors and pests; (12) permafrost thaw and microbial release of CO2 and CH4.
